subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Ultimatum Game
description: A quick, practical guide to The Ultimatum Game.

hook.text: You receive $100 to split with a stranger. You offer $1 and keep $99. The stranger rejects it, and you both get nothing.

buildup.text: In the ultimatum game, one player proposes a split and the other accepts or rejects. Rejection means both get zero.

discovery.text: Rational theory says accept any offer above zero. Experiments show offers below 20% are usually rejected.

twist.text: Offers vary by culture. The Machiguenga in Peru offer about 15%. American students offer about 45%.

climax.text: The ultimatum game proves humans are not pure profit maximizers. We punish unfairness even at personal cost.

punchline.text: We burn money to punish greed. Fairness is that powerful.

quiz.question: Why do people reject low offers in the ultimatum game?
options: They do not understand they will also get nothing
They prefer punishment of unfairness over personal profit
The game rules require rejection of low offers

details.summary: In the ultimatum game, a proposer offers a division of money that the responder can accept or reject, destroying both shares. Rational theory predicts minimal offers and acceptance, but most proposers offer 40 to 50 percent and low offers are rejected.
details.whyItMatters: The ultimatum game is the most influential experiment in behavioral economics, decisively disproving the rational self-interest model. It demonstrates that fairness concerns are so strong that people sacrifice money to punish perceived injustice.
takeaways: Proposers typically offer 40 to 50 percent, not the predicted minimum
Offers below 20 percent are rejected roughly half the time
Rejection sacrifices real money to punish perceived unfairness

faq.question: Why do people reject low offers even though it costs them?
faq.answer: Rejecting a low offer punishes the proposer for unfairness. Brain imaging shows low offers trigger disgust responses. People value self-respect and fairness enforcement enough to sacrifice material gain to uphold these principles.

faq.question: Do cultural backgrounds change ultimatum game behavior?
faq.answer: Substantially. Cross-cultural studies found offer levels ranging from 26 to 58 percent across 15 societies. Market-integrated societies with more exchange norms tend to make fairer offers, suggesting culture shapes fairness intuitions.
